0.answer: THE CLIENT owns it. ODoutreach does not send from an OpensDoors domain on the live path: it sends as the client, through the client's OWN connected Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace mailbox via Graph / Gmail API, so the From: address, the sending domain and its reputation all belong to the client. OpensDoors owns only the app domain (opensdoors.bidlow.co.uk) — which is precisely why putting a link on that domain into a client-From: email was the quarantine root cause, and why it has now been removed. CONSEQUENCE: reputation damage lands on the CLIENT's ordinary business email, not on a disposable OpensDoors sending domain. That is exactly why the volume cap and the warm-up ramp are not optional extras. DRAFTED FROM THE RECORD FOR GREG TO CONFIRM rather than asked cold — this is his stated architecture, restated from the code.

1.answer: NO — and that refusal is the defining constraint of this product, not an obstacle to route around. Greg has stated the OpensDoors owner does not want to require clients to add DNS records, and has called it the main open problem on the project. THE ENGINEERING ANSWER IS feat/zero-dns-send-profile, MERGED 2026-08-22. It works because sending through the client's own Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace mailbox means SPF, DKIM and DMARC ALREADY PASS on the client's own domain — the provider signs the mail, exactly as it signs their ordinary Outlook or Gmail. No customer DNS change is needed for AUTHENTICATION. What actually broke was never authentication: it was LINK ALIGNMENT — an email From: the client's domain carrying an unsubscribe link on opensdoors.bidlow.co.uk, which is the textbook phishing pattern. The merged branch removes the app-domain fallback entirely, stops importing resolvePublicBaseUrl into that module so it cannot return by accident, and falls back to a mailto opt-out on the sending mailbox, so a compliant send now carries NO host other than the sender's own. RESIDUAL, stated plainly: a client who wants HOSTED one-click unsubscribe or click tracking still needs one CNAME for an aligned link domain (go.<their-domain>). Zero-DNS buys correct, authenticated, non-phishing sends; it does not buy hosted links. DRAFTED FOR GREG TO CONFIRM.

2.answer: NO — there is no separate sending subdomain, and that follows from the zero-DNS decision already taken and shipped, not from a fresh choice. Sends leave through the client's EXISTING Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace mailbox, which sits on their ROOT domain. That is exactly what makes SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass with no customer DNS change — the mailbox provider signs the mail on the root domain. CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly rather than buried: the client's ORDINARY business email domain carries the whole reputation risk, because there is no disposable sending subdomain to absorb it. A bad campaign degrades the domain their invoices and customer replies travel on. That is precisely why the warm-up ramp (MAILBOX_WARMUP_RAMP=on) and the 20/day volume cap are load-bearing controls here rather than nice-to-haves, and why the generic industry advice to 'use a subdomain' cannot simply be adopted: moving to a sending subdomain would mean provisioning NEW mailboxes on mail.<client-domain> and having the client sign in to them, which is a different product shape, not a configuration setting. RECORDED AS A DECISION ALREADY TAKEN AND IMPLEMENTED — Greg to confirm the record is accurate, not to make the choice again. If he wants the subdomain shape, that is a scoped piece of work with a client-onboarding cost, and it is a ONE-WAY DOOR once mailboxes exist.

3.answer: 30 days minimum from zero, per mailbox. Researched ramp: week 1 at 5-10/day to highly engaged recipients only, week 2 at 20-30, week 3 at 50-75 rising ~15% every 2-3 days, week 4 at 100-150; normal volume only after that, and only while monitoring. ENFORCED IN CODE, not by an operator: src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup.ts computes an effective daily cap from mailbox age (WARMUP_BASE_CAP 5, +5 every 5 days) and send-introduction.ts and controlled-pilot-send.ts both call effectiveDailyCap before dispatch. It is gated by env MAILBOX_WARMUP_RAMP === 'on'; with the flag off the steady cap applies and there is no ramp. CONFIRMED 2026-08-23: MAILBOX_WARMUP_RAMP is set to 'on' in Azure App Service config on app-opensdoors-outreach-prod, read directly from the live setting. The enforcement half of this answer is therefore evidenced, not assumed.

4.answer: ODoutreach does not send through a bulk ESP on the live path: it sends as the client, through their own connected Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace mailbox (Graph / Gmail API), so the governing limit is the MAILBOX provider's, not an ESP quota. The product's own enforced ceiling is 5 mailboxes per client at 30 sends/mailbox/day, which is deliberately tighter than the researched industry norm of 4-6 mailboxes at 40-50/day (~200/day/domain). CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden: Microsoft's and Google's own published per-mailbox limits were NOT re-verified against their primary documentation in this session. The figure above is the product's self-imposed cap, which is the number that actually binds today, but the provider ceiling behind it is owed a dated primary-source check before volume rises.

5.answer: Unsubscribes: immediate and durable. A hosted one-click opt-out is minted only on a client-aligned link domain; with none configured the send carries a mailto opt-out on the sending mailbox, and replies are ingested and classified by classifyOptOutReply, which writes a suppression row. evaluateSuppression is re-checked at dispatch, so an opt-out registered between queue and send still blocks. Complaints: a spam-complaint path writes a suppression row (audit L2). Bounces: THIS IS THE WEAK LEG. Hard bounces suppress via suppressRecipientForHardBounce (append-only, idempotent) and BOUNCE_SUPPRESSION_ENABLED is on in production, but that only acts on a bounce someone has DETECTED. For the live mailbox path there is no provider delivery webhook; detection is by NDR/DSN bounce-back parsed out of the connected mailbox during inbox sync (src/server/mailbox/bounce-detection.ts, wired into mailbox-inbox-sync.ts) - and that is gated by MAILBOX_BOUNCE_DETECTION_ENABLED, which DEFAULTS OFF in code and was undocumented (added to .env.example 2026-08-23). CORRECTION, 2026-08-23: the flag is SET TO true in Azure App Service config on app-opensdoors-outreach-prod, verified by reading the live setting, as are MAILBOX_COMPLAINT_DETECTION_ENABLED and BOUNCE_SUPPRESSION_ENABLED. So the earlier inference - that a reported 0% bounce rate across ~1,209 sends was explained by the detector being switched off - is WRONG and is withdrawn. Detection is on. The 0% is therefore either genuine (hand-checked lists really do bounce near zero) or the detector is not matching NDRs back to the sent rows. That cannot be settled without production data, so it stays an OPEN question and the volume cap stands on the strength of the uncertainty rather than on a diagnosis. Timing: suppression is immediate on detection; detection is bounded by the reply-sync cron, which runs every 15 minutes on weekdays.

6.answer: There is NO separate tracking domain — and at present there is no open tracking at all: OPEN_TRACKING_PIXEL is set to 'off' in Azure App Service config on app-opensdoors-outreach-prod, read live on 2026-08-23, so buildOpenTrackingPixelUrl returns null and no pixel is embedded in any outgoing mail. WHEN IT IS ENABLED, the pixel is deliberately served from the SAME domain family as the sender: callers pass the client's aligned link domain (go.<client-domain>) as preferredBaseUrl, falling back to the app domain only for internal and governed-test rows. That is a deliberate inversion of the generic 'use a separate tracking domain' advice, and it is the right call here: a pixel on an unrelated host inside an email whose From: is the client's domain is the SAME cross-domain misalignment signal that caused the 2026 quarantine. A separate tracking domain would reintroduce the defect the zero-DNS work removed. There is a stricter setting, OPEN_TRACKING_REQUIRE_ALIGNED_DOMAIN, which suppresses the pixel entirely rather than emit a cross-domain one; it is currently UNSET (off) in production — inert while OPEN_TRACKING_PIXEL is off, but it should be turned ON at the same time tracking is ever turned back on, or the fallback to the app domain becomes reachable again. RECORDED FROM THE SHIPPED BEHAVIOUR for Greg to confirm; the open decision is only whether to re-enable tracking at all.

7.answer: NO. NOTHING STOPS SENDING AUTOMATICALLY ON A REPUTATION OR BOUNCE SIGNAL. A person has to notice. Verified by reading every consumer of the metric: bounceRate is computed in src/lib/reports/outreach-metrics.ts and rendered in exactly two places — the client Activity page and the Reports page — and no send path anywhere reads it. There is no threshold constant, no scheduled reputation check, no auto-pause. What DOES stop a send is all per-recipient or per-mailbox, and none of it is rate-aware: suppression / DNC / unsubscribe / hard-bounce on that ONE address; the per-mailbox daily cap; the warm-up ramp by mailbox age; the manual isSendingEnabled toggle; and pausing or archiving the client. So a list bouncing at 30% is stopped only by whoever happens to look at the Activity page. THIS IS THE REASON THE VOLUME CAP EXISTS: with no automatic circuit breaker, a low absolute ceiling is the only thing bounding the damage between a problem starting and a human seeing it. An automatic halt on a rolling bounce/complaint threshold is the obvious next control, and it is NOT built.

(a) PROSPECT IDENTITY AND CONTACT DETAIL, per Contact: email, fullName, firstName, lastName, company, title, linkedIn, mobilePhone, officePhone, location, city, country, industry, emailDomain, source. Mirrored and DEDUPLICATED ACROSS ALL CLIENTS in ContactUniverse (emailNormalized, linkedinUrlNormalized, mobilePhoneNormalized, officePhoneNormalized) — the warehouse is cross-tenant by design, so one prospect may appear under several clients. (b) ENRICHMENT BOUGHT FROM A THIRD PARTY: RocketReachEnrichment holds a raw JSON payload from an external data broker. (c) OUTBOUND CONTENT: OutboundEmail holds toEmail, toDomain, fromAddress, subject and bodySnapshot — the FULL sent body — plus provider ids and failure reasons. (d) INBOUND CONTENT, the widest category: InboundMailboxMessage holds fromEmail, toEmail, subject, snippet, bodyPreview and bodyText — the FULL TEXT of messages fetched from the client's connected mailbox — and InboundReply holds fromEmail, toEmail, subject, snippet, bodyPreview. (e) STAFF: StaffUser email, displayName and Entra object id. (f) SUPPRESSION: SuppressedEmail / SuppressedDomain — a record that a named person asked not to be contacted, which is itself personal data, and the one category that must OUTLIVE erasure of the rest. SPECIAL CATEGORY DATA — the honest risk: nothing in (d) is filtered by content. A prospect replying to a cold email can disclose anything — ill health, a bereavement, trade-union or political affiliation — and it is stored verbatim in bodyText, with no special handling, no flagging, and no retention limit (see Q4: there is no retention policy at all). The system does not SEEK special-category data; it will nonetheless accumulate it. No children's data is sought — the product is B2B outreach to named business contacts.

1.answer: UK PECR Regulation 22 plus UK GDPR. The distinction that governs is the recipient's LEGAL STRUCTURE, not whether they are 'a business': limited companies, LLPs and public bodies are corporate subscribers and need no prior consent, while sole traders, unincorporated partnerships and personal addresses are individual subscribers and need consent or soft opt-in exactly as consumers do. A one-person limited company falls under the carve-out; a sole trader does not. Always required regardless: truthful sender identification and a functional opt-out honoured across all future campaigns. UK GDPR sits on top - a work email address is personal data, and the lawful basis for B2B outreach is normally legitimate interests, which requires a DOCUMENTED balancing assessment (genuine purpose, proportionality, interest outweighing the recipient's rights). KNOWN PRODUCT GAP, named in the brief and still true in the code on 2026-08-22: the contact-import pipeline cannot distinguish a corporate subscriber from an individual subscriber, so the PECR consent question cannot currently be answered per recipient.

2.answer: UK/EU. The data is prospect contact data on UK businesses processed under UK GDPR, and the deployment is Azure App Service + Azure Database for PostgreSQL in the OpensDoors production resource group (rg-opensdoors-outreach-prod). UK GDPR does not mandate UK-only residency, but transfers outside the UK need a transfer mechanism, so the practical rule is: keep the database in the UK South / UK West region and do not introduce a processor that moves it. CAVEAT: the Azure region actually configured for the production database was NOT verified in this session - it is an Azure portal check, and it decides whether this answer is a description or a claim. Data residency is a listed one-way door, so it should be confirmed rather than assumed.

3.answer: There is no retention policy expressed in the code. Nothing in the schema or in any scheduled job deletes prospect data on age: Contact, OutboundEmail and InboundReply rows persist indefinitely, and the only deletion path is the super-admin workspace soft-delete/purge. Suppression must outlive the contact record it refers to, or deleting a contact silently un-suppresses them. NOTE, and this cuts against the usual 'suppression is append-only' shorthand: only the hard-bounce path is append-only. Google-Sheet-sourced suppression is REPLACE-ON-SYNC - suppression-sync.ts deleteMany's every SuppressedEmail and SuppressedDomain row for that sourceId and rewrites from the sheet, so an address removed from the client's sheet becomes sendable again. There is a shrink warning, but it warns rather than blocks. What SHOULD force deletion under UK GDPR storage limitation is a defined purpose-linked period (prospect data kept no longer than the outreach purpose needs) plus erasure on request; neither is implemented. Retention is a listed one-way door and it is currently UNSETTLED - which is a finding, not an answer, and it is why this domain still blocks.

4.answer: PARTIALLY — and the gap is named rather than smoothed over. Greg confirmed on 2026-08-23: MICROSOFT and GOOGLE are covered. Their standard data-processing terms (the Microsoft Products and Services Data Protection Addendum, and the Google Workspace / Cloud Data Processing Amendment) are incorporated into the business service terms for a paying customer without a separate signature, so Azure as host and database, Microsoft Graph as transport, and Google Workspace/Gmail plus Google Sheets as transport and suppression sync are all under a DPA. THREE ARE NOT VERIFIED and are an OPEN Art.28 OBLIGATION: (1) SENTRY — error monitoring, which can capture request context and therefore personal data, and which is a US-based processor so the transfer mechanism matters as well as the contract; (2) ROCKETREACH — the enrichment data broker, and the sharper problem of the two, because it raises a CONTROLLER question as well as a processor one: what is the lawful basis of the prospect data being BOUGHT, and can that basis be relied on downstream; (3) RESEND — the legacy fallback mail path. Resend carries no live prospect traffic today (every real send goes through a connected client mailbox via execute-one.ts, which has no ESP fallback), so its exposure is limited to non-mailbox system mail, but it is still in the chain until it is removed from the code. UK GDPR Art.28(3) requires the written contract to be in place BEFORE the processor processes personal data on the controller's behalf, so these three are outstanding NOW, not at some later compliance milestone. RECOMMENDED ORDER: RocketReach first (largest volume of prospect data and the lawful-basis question), Sentry second, and either sign or delete Resend.

1.answer: APPLICATION CODE ONLY, and it does not isolate between staff. There is no Postgres row-level security anywhere in the schema or migrations. The single read-side control is getAccessibleClientIds (src/server/tenant/access.ts), which DISCARDS its `staff` argument and returns every client with deletedAt: null - so the only wall it builds is live-vs-soft-deleted, not tenant-vs-tenant. ClientMembership exists and is written by the membership actions, but no read path consults it; only three mutator-access helpers (email-sequences, email-templates, mailbox-identities) read it, and those gate WRITES. Proven live on 2026-08-22: a staff user who is a member of Client B only opened Client A's workspace overview, its activity feed (real prospect address plus subject line) and its outbound email detail, all HTTP 200 with full data. The unit test that appears to cover this (src/server/tenant/access.test.ts) mocks prisma.client.findMany, so it never sees the where clause that is the whole control and stays green with isolation on or off. e2e/cross-tenant.spec.ts is the only thing that detects it, and it is RED.

3.answer: EVERY active staff member can see across every live tenant, and it is NOT logged per access. This is by design, not a defect: ODoutreach was built as an internal OpensDoors tool where all staff are one company, and in-account roles were deliberately removed in 2026-06. GREG'S DECISION, 2026-08-23: this design stands and the 64-call-site isolation project is NOT to be started. The pilot is separated at the DEPLOYMENT level instead - one instance per client organisation - so no staff member reads another organisation's prospects. CONSEQUENCE TO STATE PLAINLY, and it is a commercial constraint rather than a bug: selling a SHARED instance to two clients who must not see each other is a REBUILD, not a feature. Nothing about the current product should be sold on a claim of tenant isolation between staff users.

4.answer: A tenant is SOFT-deleted: Client.deletedAt is stamped, which removes it from getAccessibleClientIds and therefore from every normal read path, and the capability is gated on the per-account isSuperAdmin flag (canDeleteWorkspace), not on a role enum or an email string. A separate explicit hard purge follows. Everything is retained until that purge - contacts, outbound emails, replies - so a soft-delete is recoverable and is NOT an erasure under UK GDPR. That matters because there is no retention policy in code either (see regulated_data Q4), so 'deleted' currently means 'hidden from staff', and should not be described to a client as anything stronger. FOR GREG TO CONFIRM: whether that is the intended contractual meaning of deleting a workspace.

Errors are returned INSIDE an HTTP 200 body, so the workflow goes green while real faults accumulate - 8 of 35 mailboxes failing reply sync, a long errors array, and one mailbox not eligible for sending, all inside a successful response. 2.answer: YES for the paths that matter, and it is enforced rather than assumed. Suppression is APPEND-ONLY and idempotent (suppressRecipientForHardBounce refreshes a timestamp on an existing row rather than duplicating, and audits only the first time). Dispatch re-checks suppression and bounces before sending, so a repeated run cannot re-send a suppressed address. The known exception is sheet-sourced suppression, which is REPLACE-ON-SYNC rather than append-only - removing a row from the client's sheet makes that address sendable again.

0.answer: Microsoft Graph and the Gmail API by OAuth, for sending as the client and reading their inbox - this is the whole zero-DNS architecture. Google Sheets by OAuth for each client's do-not-contact list. RocketReach by API for contact enrichment. Resend by API and webhook for system mail only - a transport guard REFUSES to route prospect outreach through it. Sentry by SDK for error monitoring.

1.answer: THE CLIENT owns the mailbox credentials: OAuth tokens are issued against the client's own Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace tenant and stored per ClientMailboxIdentity. When they expire or are revoked the mailbox stops sending and the row FAILS rather than rerouting - there is no ESP fallback. The honest gap: how often that happens, and who notices, is recorded as UNKNOWN rather than as zero, and one such failure was visible today as mailbox_oauth=error&reason=callback_failed.

2.answer: IT CARRIES ON, DELIBERATELY, AND DOES NOT CATCH UP IN A BURST. [stated] Greg, verbatim: "carry on but avoid burst sends when they come back online again." Implemented as paced sending - four at a time with gaps, configured per client - so a backlog drains at a human rate instead of arriving as a spike that damages the sending reputation.
2.source: PR #270 'Paced sending: four at a time with gaps, set per client, and switched on', with the property pinned by a test in PR #272; and Greg Visser, recorded verbatim during classification, 2026-08-24. Re-entered 2026-08-27 after a rebase reverted the working tree; the wording is his, not a paraphrase.

3.answer: WHAT IS ENFORCED IN THE PRODUCT, cited: a per-mailbox DAILY CAP with a warm-up ramp starting at 5 a day and rising by 5 every 5 days by mailbox age, with a slot reserved against that cap before an OutboundEmail row is written. Target steady state is 30 a day per mailbox. THE HONEST GAP, stated rather than invented: the PROVIDER-side ceilings for Microsoft Graph and the Gmail API are NOT cited with a date anywhere in this repo, and the '<2% bounce' figure that GRADES.json calls non-negotiable was checked on 2026-08-24 and has no primary source - Google publishes no bounce threshold at all, only a complaint rate below 0.10%. Recorded in _open_obligations rather than filled in with a number nobody checked.

1.answer: An OutboundEmail moves QUEUED -> SENT -> DELIVERED / REPLIED / BOUNCED / FAILED / BLOCKED_SUPPRESSION, and the mover is the system, not a person: the scheduled dispatcher sends it, the reply sync links replies and bounces. A sequence is moved Draft -> Approved -> Launched -> Archived by a STAFF member. A contact is moved to Suppressed by the system (bounce, unsubscribe, sheet sync) or by a staff member manually. Archiving a sequence stops it sending and deletes nothing.

0.answer: NOT FOR BILLING - nothing in the product bills anyone. FOR COMPLIANCE, YES, and that is why it matters: the bounce rate is the number a client judges deliverability by, and send proof (providerMessageId + sentAt) is the record that an email was really sent. That is exactly why the bounce rate reading a flat 0% across 1,209 sends was treated as a customer-ready blocker rather than a cosmetic bug, and fixed on 2026-08-27.
